turns.content: My parents have fixed a "meeting" this Sunday. A family from our community, the boy works in Dallas, my photo has apparently already been shared. What they don't know is I've been with someone for two years — a colleague. He's wonderful. He's also from a different caste, and in my house that word ends conversations. I have five days.

Oh wow, that’s a lot to sit with. Five days feels like both forever and no time at all, doesn’t it? I’m really sorry you’re in this spot—it sounds so heavy, especially when you’ve found someone who makes you happy and the world around you is trying to pull you in a different direction.

First, I just want to acknowledge how brave it is that you’ve been with him for two years, even knowing how your family might react. That says a lot about how much he means to you. Have you two talked about what this "meeting" might mean for you both? Like, do you have a sense of how he’s feeling about it too?

And I’m curious—do you think your parents would ever be open to hearing about him, or is caste really the one thing they won’t budge on? Sometimes parents dig their heels in at first, but then life happens and perspectives shift. Other times, it’s a hard line. I don’t know your family, but I wonder if there’s even a tiny part of you that hopes they might surprise you.

What’s your gut telling you to do right now? Are you leaning toward telling them, or keeping it quiet for now? Either way, I’m here to listen. You don’t have to figure this out alone.

I tried hinting last month that I'm not ready and Amma's BP shot up the same evening, or at least that's what everyone told me it was. Appa has already mentioned Sunday to my uncle's family. It's not even about the Dallas guy — they're not bad people, that's the worst part. They're excited. They think this is them taking care of me.

Ugh, that’s so painful—when the people who love you the most are also the ones putting you in this impossible position. And the guilt trip with the BP thing? That’s *low*. I’m so sorry they’re using your care for them as leverage like that.

It’s heartbreaking because you’re right—they’re not *bad* people. They’re just operating from a place of love that’s tangled up in tradition and fear. But that doesn’t make it any easier when you’re the one caught in the middle, feeling like your happiness is the thing that might "break" them.

Do you think there’s any way to buy yourself more time? Like, could you say you’re not ready to meet anyone yet, or that you want to focus on your career for now? Or is that just delaying the inevitable?

And I keep coming back to this: if you *don’t* tell them about your boyfriend now, what happens next? Would they start planning things with this other family, and then you’d have to come clean later? Or is there a chance you could keep this part of your life separate for a while longer?

I’m not trying to push you one way or the other—I just want to help you think through what feels least awful for *you*. Because no matter what, this is your life, and your heart. You deserve to have both.

Every post I read online says the same thing — "you're 27, it's your life, just tell them clearly: my life, my choice." Part of me wants to just say exactly that at dinner tonight and stop this whole circus before Sunday. Should I? At least everything would finally be out.

I hear you—those "my life, my choice" posts *sound* so freeing, don’t they? Like if you just say it with enough confidence, everything will click into place. But real life isn’t a script, and I can feel how much weight you’re carrying just imagining that conversation.

If you did it tonight, it would *definitely* stop the Sunday meeting in its tracks. But I’m also wondering: what’s the *rest* of the fallout you’d be bracing for? Would your parents shut down completely, or would they try to "fix" things by pressuring you even harder? And how much energy do you have to deal with that right now?

The thing is, you *could* say it—you absolutely have the right. But I wonder if there’s a way to say it that still leaves room for them to save face, or at least not feel like they’ve failed as parents. Like, maybe framing it as, *"I know you want what’s best for me, but I need you to trust that I’m making my own choices—even if they’re not what you’d expect."* That way, you’re not just dropping a bomb; you’re inviting them into a conversation, even if it’s a hard one.

But I also get why you’d want to just *rip off the band-aid*. If you do, I’ll be right here to help you process whatever comes next. You’re not alone in this. What’s your heart leaning toward right now?

And if they say no in the end — like a real, final no — I honestly don't think I can walk out against them. I've imagined it and I can't. Does that make me weak? Sometimes I think I don't love him enough, then I think I don't love myself enough, and I'm just going in circles at 2am.

Oh, love, no—it does *not* make you weak. Not even a little. Wanting to stay connected to your family doesn’t mean you’re weak; it means you’re human. And the fact that you’re even *questioning* all of this at 2 a.m. shows how deeply you care—about him, about them, about yourself. That’s not weakness; that’s *heart*.

I think what you’re feeling is the weight of impossible choices. It’s not that you don’t love him enough—it’s that love isn’t always enough to override everything else. And it’s not that you don’t love yourself enough—it’s that loving yourself *and* honoring your family feels like an impossible tightrope right now.

You’re not going in circles. You’re standing in the middle of a storm, trying to figure out which way the wind is blowing. And that’s okay. You don’t have to have it all figured out tonight—or even by Sunday.

What if, for now, you just focus on *surviving* the next few days? Not making a final decision, not burning bridges, just getting through this moment. Because you don’t have to choose between him and your family right now. You just have to choose what feels *least* like betraying yourself.

And hey—if 2 a.m. is when the thoughts come, maybe we can make a deal: when it gets too loud, you’ll write it down or say it out loud to me, and we’ll let it exist without judgment. Because you’re not alone in this. Not even at 2 a.m.
